title: 1989: The Wall Falls

cards.h: A press conference mistake ended a divided Europe
cards.b:
On the evening of 9 November 1989, East German official Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules. Asked when they took effect, he shuffled his notes and said, 'immediately, without delay'. He had not been told it was meant for the next day.

Crowds rushed to the Berlin Wall. Guards, overwhelmed, opened the gates.
In Poland, the union Solidarity won the June 1989 elections. In summer Hungary opened its border with Austria, and thousands of East Germans left through it.

Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet leader from 1985, began glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring). Crucially, he refused to use Soviet tanks to prop up Eastern European regimes, unlike in 1956 and 1968.

So one by one, the regimes fell, mostly peacefully: the 'Velvet Revolution' in Czechoslovakia, and bloody in Romania, where Ceausescu was shot on 25 December.

In China, the 1989 Tiananmen protests were crushed on 4 June. Beijing's leaders chose force and kept power. It shows the outcome was not inevitable.

Germany reunified on 3 October 1990.

Weakened by economics and nationalism, the USSR itself broke up. In August 1991 hardliners attempted a coup and failed. Boris Yeltsin rose. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned and the USSR dissolved into 15 states.

Some credit Reagan's pressure and his 1987 call 'Mr Gorbachev, tear down this wall'. Others credit Gorbachev's choices, the weak Soviet economy, or ordinary people in the streets. Most historians say many causes combined.

Myth check: the Wall did not fall in one night by hand; much of it was pulled down over the following months and years.

Five things to remember

  1. Eastern Europe's regimes fell in 1989.
  2. Gorbachev refused to use force.
  3. The Wall opened on 9 November 1989.
  4. Germany reunified in 1990; the USSR ended in 1991.
  5. India liberalised in 1991.

Think about it

  • Was it inevitable or lucky?
  • Why did China differ?

sources: Sarotte, 1989: The Struggle to Create Post-Cold War Europe (2009); Kotkin, Armageddon Averted; Gorbachev, Memoirs; Ahluwalia on 1991 reforms
